title: The best of stories
hook: We tell you the best of stories (12:3)

segments.voice: Yesterday, islah, Shu'ayb's reform, as far as he was able. Your line was only to set things right. What small thing did you quietly fix? Day four hundred thirty-nine.

Surah Hud ended with prophet after prophet and people after people who would not listen. It's heavy. The next surah opens differently. It opens like someone settling into a chair by the fire. We tell you, it says, the best of stories. You've met Yusuf already on this path: the dream of the eleven stars, the well, the prison, the palace. Now we come back to him with a different question. Not what happens. Why does this surah open by speaking of the best of stories?
screen: `WE TELL YOU THE BEST OF STORIES.`

segments.voice: Verse three, in Pickthall's translation, begins: "We narrate unto thee (Muhammad) the best of narratives". In Arabic, ahsan al-qasas. Qasas can mean the stories themselves, or the act of telling them, so commentators have read it both ways: the best of stories, or the best way of telling. Commentators also differ on what the phrase points to: some take it as the story of Yusuf that follows, others as the Qur'an's telling as a whole. Some commentators place the surah in a hard stretch of the Prophet's years in Mecca, around the time he lost his wife Khadija and his uncle Abu Talib, when the small community was under heavy pressure. And here is a story about a boy betrayed by his brothers, sold, slandered, jailed, forgotten, who ends up with power over the very people who wronged him. So what makes it best? Commentators give answers that stack. It's complete: one prophet's story told from beginning to end in a single surah. It has every kind of person in it: prophets and kings, a jealous family, a woman who tries to seduce and later confesses, a prisoner, a merchant, a grieving father. It has every kind of trial: envy, temptation, injustice, long separation, grief that whitens a father's eyes. And it ends not in destruction, like the stories in Hud, but in a family reunited and a sentence of forgiveness. When the brothers finally stand before him, Yusuf says: no reproach on you today. The best of stories is the one where the wronged man, with all the power in the room, chooses mercy.
screen: `AHSAN AL-QASAS.` · `TOLD IN A HARD YEAR.` · `EVERY KIND OF PERSON, EVERY TRIAL.` · `NO REPROACH ON YOU TODAY.` · then, large: `THE BEST OF STORIES.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: retell Yusuf's story to someone. Sit first, and breathe. In your mind, run the story in five pictures: the dream, the well, the prison, the palace, the brothers bowing. Which picture do you feel most? Then think of who you could tell it to today: a child at bedtime, a friend going through a betrayal, a parent. Picture telling it in two minutes, ending with: no reproach on you today. The bell holds the time.
The best of stories. Ahsan al-qasas, the phrase that opens the story of Yusuf, read as the best of stories or the best way of telling. Today's word.
Your line: the best of stories. Today, tell Yusuf's story, or one piece of it, to one person, out loud. Day four hundred thirty-nine.

howItsDone: Surah Yusuf is often retold; parents tell it to children, and teachers use it to speak about patience, temptation and forgiveness within families.

original.note: Arabic: "the best of stories" (12:3); qasas is both the stories and the telling.

trapdoor: what you thought: the Qur'an's most dramatic story.
what it means: a complete story of every trial that ends in forgiveness, called the best of stories.
what a scholar hears: qasas is a verbal noun, so ahsan al-qasas may mean 'the finest narration'; Surah Yusuf is usually dated to the late Meccan period, near the 'year of sorrow.'

notes: Pickthall wording of 12:3 quoted from memory; please confirm exactly.
Dating Surah Yusuf to the period around the deaths of Khadija and Abu Talib ('year of sorrow') is a common view, not certain; the script says 'many place'. Confirm.
The two readings of ahsan al-qasas (best stories / best telling) are from the tafsir tradition (e.g. az-Zamakhshari, ar-Razi); confirm.
